blocks.text: I. Jonathan and the Syriac explain it as ܣܪܩܪܩܐ serakreka; and Onkelos as ירקרקא jerakreka. I think these are the same, although the former is named from a hissing sound, the latter from a green colour. The Talmudists too render it שרקרק serakrak. The passage is in the tractate Cholin, fol. 63a: רחם זו שרקרק אמר רבי יוחנן למה נקרא שמו רחם כיון שבא רחם באו רחמים לעולם, "Racham is the same bird as serakrak. Rabbi Johanan said: Why is it called racham? (That is, why was it given a name from mercy, which in Hebrew is רחם?) When racham comes, mercies come into the world." And there the Gloss says: רחמים מטר, Mercies, that is, rain, which God [III, 49] grants us in his kindness, according to the words of Luke in Act. XIV, 16: He did not leave himself without witness, ἀγαθοποιῶν [agathopoiōn] doing good, giving us rains from heaven. In the same place they teach that שרקרק serakrak is named from its cry. For there follows: אמר רב בבי בר אביי והוא דיתיב אמידי ועביד שרקרק, Rabbi Bibi, son of Abii, said: It is a bird which, wherever it sits, makes serakrak; that is, it seems to utter this with its whistling. They add: דאי יתיב בארעא ושריק אתי משיחא שנאמר אשרקה להם ואקבצם, When it sits on the ground whistling, the Messiah will come, as it is said Zachar. X, 8: "I will whistle [col. 298] for them and gather them." The bird, that is, is believed to be of good omen; and, as the Glossator has it, when it does not stand but sits and whistles, סימן בשורה הוא, it is a sign of good tidings, especially if it sits on the ground, שאין דרכו, which it does contrary to its habit. So when that bird sits and whistles thus, or when God himself whistles through that bird, if we believe the circumcised doctors, the Jewish Messiah will come, and the Jews, scattered over the whole world, will be gathered according to the prophecy just cited, I will whistle for them and gather them. It therefore matters a great deal to them to know what bird this is, and yet they are wholly ignorant of it. For the Jews of Germany, as Münster and Fagius testify, interpret it as the magpie. Münster follows this in his Latin version, and Diodati in his Italian. And it may seem probable, since in Gesner Gratarolus says that the magpie was called by the ancients the rain bird, because when it chatters more than usual it is a sure sign of a shower. And the modern name of the magpie, καρακάξα [karakaxa], used by the Greeks today, comes close to serakraka. Yet the descriptions of the Arabs show that it differs from the magpie. They call the same bird شرقراق [shirqirāq] sirikrak, and by metathesis شقراق [shiqirrāq] sikirrak, and شرشاق [shirshāq] sirisak; and in Alcamus they define it: طاير مرقط بخضرة وحمرة وبياض ويكون بارض الاحرام [ṭāyir muraqqaṭ bi-khuḍra wa-ḥumra wa-bayāḍ wa-yakūnu bi-arḍ al-aḥrām] A bird spotted with green, red and white, which is found in the land of Alachram, that is, around Mecca and Medina ^{(1)}. And in Alkazuinius: طاير يقال له بالفارسية [III, 50] كاسينة اخضر اللون احمر المنقار وقد يكون اصغر عدو النحل ياكل منها ويقتل ما لا ياكل [ṭāyir yuqālu lahu bi-l-fārisiyya kāsīna akhḍar al-lawn aḥmar al-minqār wa-qad yakūnu aṣfar ʿadūw al-naḥl yaʾkulu minhā wa-yaqtulu mā lā yaʾkulu] A bird which in Persian is called CASINA, green in the colour of its feathers, with a red beak, sometimes also yellow; hostile to bees, which it swallows, and it even kills those which it does not eat. And in Damir: طاير صغير يسمي الاخيل والعرب تتشام به وهو اخضر مليح بقدر الحمامة خضرته حسنة مشبعة وفي اجنحته سواد وله مشتا ومصيف يكثر في البلاد الروم والشام وخراسان ونواجد وفي طبعه شرة وشراسة وسرقة فراخ غيره وهو لا يزال الا متباعدا من الناس ويالف الروابي وروس الجبال لكنه يحضن بيضه في العمران العوالي الذي لا تناله الايدي وعشه شديد النتن [ṭāyir ṣaghīr yusammī al-akhyal wa-l-ʿarab tatashāʾamu bihi wa-huwa akhḍar malīḥ bi-qadr al-ḥamāma khuḍratuhu ḥasana mushbaʿa wa-fī ajniḥatihi sawād wa-lahu mashtā wa-maṣīf yakthuru fī al-bilād al-rūm wa-l-shām wa-khurāsān wa-nawājid wa-fī ṭabʿihi shirra wa-sharāsa wa-sariqat firākh ghayrihi wa-huwa lā yazālu illā mutabāʿidan min al-nās wa-yaʾlafu al-rawābī wa-rūs al-jibāl lākinnahu yaḥḍunu bayḍahu fī al-ʿumrān al-ʿawālī alladhī lā tanāluhu al-aydī wa-ʿushshuhu shadīd al-natn] A small bird, by another name called achial (that is, spotted, [col. 299] although for others achial is the bird صرد [ṣurad] surad, commonly the lesser shrike). The Arabs consider it ill-omened. It is green, elegant, the size of a dove. Its green is beautiful and deep. In its wings there is black. It is present both in winter and in summer. It abounds in the lands of the Greeks, Syria, Chorasan and Negid (in Arabia Felix). It is of a wicked nature and bad disposition. It steals young that are not its own. It keeps as far as possible from all company of men. It lives on hills and on the tops of mountains. And it broods its eggs in the loftiest places, which hands cannot reach. Its nest is extremely foul-smelling. Of the same bird Algiahid says: انه نوع من الغربان وفي طبعه السرقة والعفة من السفاد وهو كثير الاستغاثة اذا طار بقربه طاير ضربه وصاحْ كانه المضروب [innahu nawʿ min al-ghirbān wa-fī ṭabʿihi al-sariqa wa-l-ʿiffa min al-sifād wa-huwa kathīr al-istighātha idhā ṭāra bi-qurbihi ṭāyir ḍarabahu wa-ṣāḥa kaʾannahu al-maḍrūb], That it is a species of raven, of a thievish nature, much abstaining from coition, and querulous and clamorous, so that if another bird flies near, it beats it and cries out as if it had itself been beaten. Some of the Arabs permit eating it, others forbid it, لاستخباثه [li-istikhbāthihi] because of its foulness. Yet Avicenna commends it in these words in book 2 of the Canon, in the chapter On meats: لحم الشقراق كاسر [III, 51] الرياح وابعد اللحمان من تعفن اقله شحما وايبسه جوهرا [laḥm al-shiqirrāq kāsir al-riyāḥ wa-abʿad al-luḥmān min taʿaffun aqalluhu shaḥman wa-aybasuhu jawharan] The flesh of the sikirrak dispels flatulence, and since it has little fat and a very dry substance, it is the furthest of all from corruption. In the Paroemiographers this proverb about that bird occurs: اشام من الاخيل وهو الشقراق [ashʾam min al-akhyal wa-huwa al-shiqirrāq] More ill-omened than the bird achial, that is, the bird sikirrak. Accordingly Damir had said above that this bird is held by the Arabs to be ill-omened. The Talmudists, however, hold on the contrary that it is a bird of good omen; but who would be surprised that in matters which depend on opinion human judgements vary? صاحب الحيل [ṣāḥib al-ḥiyal], that is, the author of the Arts, attributes to its gall a property which I cannot pass over here untouched: اذا كان الذهب ناقص العيار يذاب ويفرغ عليه من مرارته فانه يتحجر ويبردان عياره كما لو افرغ عليه مرارة الثعلب فانه ينقص عياره [idhā kāna al-dhahab nāqiṣ al-ʿiyār yudhābu wa-yufraghu ʿalayhi min marāratihi fa-innahu yataḥajjaru wa-ybrdān ʿiyāruhu kamā law afragha ʿalayhi marārat al-thaʿlab fa-innahu yanquṣu ʿiyāruhu] If gold is deficient in weight, it is melted and the gall of this bird is poured on it; and when the gold has solidified, it becomes heavier in weight. Just as, conversely, it becomes lighter if the gall of a fox is poured on it. Less wonderful is what follows: اذا اتخذ من مرارته خضاب سود الشعر [idhā ittukhidha min marāratihi khiḍāb sawwada al-shaʿr] a dye taken from that gall blackens the hair. In the plains of Tartary around the Caucasus and the Caucasian Gates, which today they call Derbend, that is, the narrows, and Temir capi, that is, the iron gate, there is an abundance of these birds, about which what Hayton the Armenian relates in his book On the Tartars, chapter 47, is worth noting: In a certain plain which is called Mon- [col. 300] ga (read Mongal) there remain in winter certain birds the size of pheasants, which have very beautiful feathers, and are called seicerach (شقراق [shiqirrāq]). Hence, when any peoples enter that plain, those birds immediately flee and pass over those guard-posts and ditches (where Derbend and the Iron Gate are, which he had treated a little before), and those who are appointed to guard that place clearly learn through those birds of the enemies' approach, and are at once prepared for defence. From all this I gather much. First, that these birds are not magpies, as the Hebrews think, and perhaps also among the Arabs Algiahid; since in bulk of body, colour of feathers and beak, food, stench, and the nest they build in the remotest mountains, they differ entirely from the magpie. Second, that they are not green woodpeckers, as a most learned man and very dear friend of mine has held, since this bird has scarcely anything in common with the woodpecker except its colour, which is green in both, but paler in the woodpecker. Third, although I cannot determine what bird شرقراق [shirqirāq] sirikrak is, because among European birds none is like it, it is nevertheless clear that it has nothing in common with the Hebrew רחם racham; and that the Talmudists, the Chaldees, the Syrians and the more recent Hebrews, who determine that racham and serakraka are the same bird, are gravely mistaken. But now others must be heard.
